From the “small people” of the Spanish court to so-called monstrous births in Italy, early modern Europe was fascinated — and unsettled — by bodily difference. In the age of exploration, when knowledge of the world was expanding rapidly, the boundaries of humanity itself became increasingly fraught. Social and aesthetic pressures placed a premium on bodies understood as beautiful, whole, and healthy, while bodies that departed from these ideals were represented, scrutinized, and often ridiculed. Art and artists were deeply implicated in these anxieties, essential to the depiction, interpretation, and cataloguing of bodily difference. Yet artists were themselves often part of these histories. From the celebrated engraver Hendrick Goltzius to the master draughtsman Guercino, there is considerable evidence that artists’ lives and practices were deeply shaped by disability. This class investigates the realities (and fractures) of disability in early modern Europe through a combination of lectures, discussion seminars, and creative workshops. Together, we will consider how disability was represented, understood, experienced, and contested, and how art might offer new ways of thinking about bodily difference in the early modern world.
sections.title: Disability in the Early Modern

sections.note: China Framed: Making Sense of Cinematic Orients. This course begins with an examination of how films primarily produced in the United States represented China. The films I have selected exemplify the racial tension that has characterized America’s China since the late 19th century and through the late 20th century. To identify the ever-shifting character of this racial tension, and how it intersected with issues of gender and class, we shall supplement our visual experience of the films with historical and literary writings. The visual culture from which the films drew will be further examined through contemporary woodblock prints, paintings, and photography. Finally, we shall consider films that were produced in late 20th-century China, Taiwan, and Hong Kong. We shall question how these last filmmakers articulated their position within an increasingly connected world, while still constructing a distinctive image of China. Above all, we shall consider how the aesthetics of all the films we view allow us to think about, and feel, the urgent ethical and political issues that face China in the world today.

sections.note: This research seminar will explore parallel modes of curatorial and scholarly engagement. Our first thematic will be “contemporary art and the shape of history.” We will consider how artists of our time engage history and historical narrative in unique and vital ways through readings, screenings, and by analyzing the stakes and meaning of contemporary art amid multiple crises and slow violences in the US and transnationally. The class coincides with part one of an exhibition series on this theme at Krannert Art Museum, and our readings and discussions will inform subsequent iterations of the project. The artists in Degrees of Archive will visit the course. Our second thematic will empower students with critical and practical tools to ask curatorial research questions, to work alongside artists and archives, and to explore avenues for exhibition-making on campus and in community. For upper-level undergraduates and graduate students. Graduate Section. Meets with section PPU.

sections.note: Sex and Sexuality in Early Modern Art. Around 1500, a profound transformation began in Europe: sex increasingly became an object of public representation and consumption. In paintings, frescoes, prints, and sculpture, the boundaries of what could and should be shown were challenged by developments such as the printing press, medical innovation, and religious upheaval. Sex had always been present in art, but its visual codes now proliferated. The satyr, the nude, the garden, and the grotesque became charged with erotic and sexual meaning. Drawing upon art history, the history of sexuality, gender studies, and social history, the course asks how sexuality was visualized, regulated, concealed, and performed in early modern art and culture. This course fulfills the seminar requirement for Art History majors and minors. Open to Juniors and Seniors, or with permission of the instructor. ARTH 395 prerequisite is only recommended, not required.

sections.note: Atlantic and Indian Ocean Africa. The cosmopolitan and commercial entrepôts of the Indian Ocean, the trans-Saharan trade routes and African Atlantic worlds are testament to Africa’s rootedness in global medieval and early modern cultural and material exchanges. While these early interactions were often unequal, they bequeathed resilient material and cultural legacies – ritual objects, trade goods, Islam, religious practices and ideas about space. These older spatial and urban forms had to contend with the assaults of European colonial and postcolonial planning schemes.

Non-Aligned Modernisms This seminar examines recent scholarship on the arts of the Non-Aligned Movement, with particular focus on Yugoslavia. When Yugoslavia broke with the Soviet Union in 1948 to pursue a novel form of socialism based on worker self-management, the rupture opened debates about what a socialist, decolonial art world might look like. We will consider the resulting experiments in museology, international exhibition practices, design, and the built environment, as well as broader efforts to build a network of transnational cultural exchange. To what extent did a “third way” modernism offer an alternative to the Cold War’s competing cultural hegemonies—Western modernism, on the one hand, and the socialist realism of the Eastern Bloc, on the other? How did the non-aligned world look and feel? What were its institutional and formal strategies? How did identification with the Global South disrupt or reproduce the dynamics of racial capitalism? While the seminar’s focus is Yugoslavia, we will also attend to some recent scholarship on non-aligned art in other geographies, and students are welcome to develop projects centered on other contexts in which they have interest/expertise.
